mainTopic: Partly upholding or cancelling a two-part vow, and a husband or father who missed the time to cancel because he did not know the law
overview: The amud opens at the end of a משנה about a woman who vowed off figs and grapes together. If her husband cancels only the figs, רבי ישמעאל says nothing is cancelled until he cancels the grapes too. רבי עקיבא learns from the פסוק that cancelling part of the vow works, just like upholding part. רבי יוחנן then reports that חכמים read the same היקש the other way: whatever he upholds or cancels covers only what he named. רבא says that the משנה's ruling, that repeating the vow word for each fruit makes two vows, follows רבי שמעון. A new משנה follows about a husband or father who let the day pass without cancelling. If he did not know vows could be cancelled, he may still cancel. If he did not know this was a vow, רבי מאיר and חכמים disagree. The גמרא then challenges these positions with a ברייתא about a blind person who kills by accident, where רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה seem to hold the reverse. The answer comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Cancelling only the figs does not work, according to רבי ישמעאל
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that if the husband cancels only the figs part of a combined vow, nothing is cancelled until he cancels the grapes too.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he cancelled the figs part, the vow is not cancelled until he also cancels the grapes part. These are the words of רבי ישמעאל.
steps.whatsHappening: We are in the middle of a משנה. A woman vowed off figs and grapes in one vow, and her husband cancelled only the figs part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just before this, the משנה taught that upholding even one part (figs) upholds the whole vow. Here it teaches the opposite direction: cancelling only one part does nothing. In רבי ישמעאל's view, a הפרה works only on the vow as a whole.

keyTerms.meaning: He cancelled (a vow of his wife or daughter)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the figs at least become permitted. According to רבי ישמעאל, cancelling only part does nothing at all. Even the figs stay forbidden until he cancels the whole vow.

phrases.english: If he nullified for figs —
phrases.notes: Earlier in this משנה, the woman vowed off figs and grapes together in one vow.

phrases.english: it is not nullified
until he nullifies also for the grapes,
these are the words of Rabbi Yishmael.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵפֵר לִתְאֵנִים אֵינוֹ מוּפָר עַד שֶׁיָּפֵר אַף לַעֲנָבִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה from the previous amud (87a) about the combined figs-and-grapes vow.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A partial הפרה of a combined vow has no effect until the whole vow is cancelled (רבי ישמעאל).

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: a husband can cancel part of a vow
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא learns from the פסוק that, just as upholding can be partial, cancelling can be partial too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: the פסוק says 'Her husband may uphold it and her husband may cancel it.' Just as 'uphold it' means part of it, so too 'cancel it' means part of it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא disagrees with רבי ישמעאל. He brings a פסוק to show that a husband can cancel just one part of the vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He reads the ending of the words יקימנו and יפרנו as if they said ממנו, 'part of it.' Both sides agree that upholding just part of the vow upholds the whole vow. רבי עקיבא says a partial act counts for cancelling too, so cancelling just the figs cancels the whole vow, grapes too, just as upholding part upholds the whole.

keyTerms.meaning: From it, meaning part of it

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says:
Behold, it says
"Her husband may uphold it, and her husband may nullify it,"
just as "may uphold it" means part of it,
phrases.notes: He reads the ending נּוּ as if it said מִמֶּנּוּ, 'from it,' meaning even part of the vow.

phrases.english: so too "may nullify it" means part of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר הֲרֵי הוּא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view to רבי ישמעאל, based on a פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A partial הפרה works, just like a partial הקמה (רבי עקיבא).

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל: the פסוק never says 'cancel part of it'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains רבי ישמעאל's side: the פסוק does not actually say יפר ממנו.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי ישמעאל would answer: is it written 'he may cancel part of it'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now speaks for רבי ישמעאל and asks how he deals with רבי עקיבא's proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל rejects reading 'part of it' into the word for cancelling. The words 'part of it' are not written there, so he limits the idea of a partial act to upholding only.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it written? A way of saying the פסוק does not say that

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yishmael [says]:
Is it written "he may nullify part of it"?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל מִי כְּתִיב יָפֵר מִמֶּנּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי עקיבא's reading of the פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי עקיבא's reading of יפרנו as 'part of it'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The words 'part of it' are not written about cancelling, so you cannot read them into the פסוק.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: the פסוק puts cancelling next to upholding
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא answers with a היקש: the פסוק links cancelling to upholding, so both can be partial.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי עקיבא answers: the פסוק compares cancelling to upholding. Just as upholding can be part of the vow, so too cancelling can be part of the vow.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא defends his view. He says he doesn't need the exact words, because the פסוק places the two actions side by side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since upholding and cancelling appear together in one פסוק, they share the same rules. This is a היקש. Upholding is partial, so cancelling is partial too.

keyTerms.meaning: Compares; links two things so they share the same rules (היקש)

phrases.english: And Rabbi Akiva [says]:
it compares nullifying to upholding,
just as upholding can be part of it,
so too nullifying can be part of it.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Source comes from a היקש, not from the exact wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The idea of 'part of it' depends on the words being written about cancelling.
steps.terutzMaskana: Putting the two actions side by side in the פסוק is enough to give cancelling the same partial rule as upholding.
steps.whatToRemember: Both רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא agree that upholding part of the vow upholds all of it. They argue only about cancelling part of it.

steps.title: חכמים: upholding is also only as much as he upheld
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן reports that חכמים compare upholding to cancelling, so upholding the figs upholds only the figs.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: this is the view of רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא. But חכמים say: the פסוק compares upholding to cancelling. Just as with cancelling, what he cancelled is cancelled, so too with upholding, what he upheld is upheld.
steps.whatsHappening: A new opinion is brought. רבי יוחנן says the rule that upholding part upholds everything is not shared by everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא used the היקש in one direction, making cancelling like upholding. חכמים use it in the other direction, making upholding like cancelling. In their view each act works only on the part he actually named.

keyTerms.meaning: What he upheld is upheld, and nothing more

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said
Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: זוֹ דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל וְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא,
phrases.english: This is the view of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva,
phrases.notes: 'This' means the rule that upholding the figs upholds the whole vow, which both of them accept.

phrases.english: but the Sages say:
it compares upholding to nullifying;
just as with nullifying, what he nullified is nullified,
so too with upholding, what he upheld is upheld.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third opinion that disagrees with the shared assumption of רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to חכמים, both upholding and cancelling apply only to the part he names.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that one היקש can be read in two directions, and the direction decides the הלכה.
steps.whatToRemember: There are three views. רבי ישמעאל: upholding part upholds all, and cancelling part does nothing. רבי עקיבא: upholding part upholds all, and cancelling part cancels that part. חכמים: each act works only on what he named.

steps.title: רבא: the 'two separate vows' ruling follows רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: On the משנה's case of 'קונם a fig... and a grape...', רבא says it follows רבי שמעון, who requires the vow word to be repeated for each item.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said that if she said 'קונם a fig (that I taste)...', these are two vows. רבא said: our משנה follows רבי שמעון, who said a person is not liable separately unless he says 'שבועה' for each one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes another line of the משנה. רבא tells us which תנא it follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה counts two vows only because she repeated her vow wording for each fruit. That matches רבי שמעון in the laws of oaths, where separate oaths count only if he says 'שבועה' to each person.

keyTerms.meaning: A word used to make a vow forbidding something

phrases.english: [The משנה teaches:] if she said "konam a fig",
phrases.notes: The full case in the משנה is 'a fig that I taste and a grape that I taste,' which counts as two vows.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Our mishna follows Rabbi Shimon.
For he said:
[One is not liable for each] unless he says "oath"
phrases.notes: This comes from the laws of oaths: someone who falsely swears to several people that he doesn't have their item.

phrases.english: to each and every one.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרָה קֻוֽנָּם תְּאֵנָה אָמַר רָבָא מַתְנִיתִין רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a different line of the משנה and identifies its author.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's 'two vows' ruling follows רבי שמעון: separate vows require repeating the vow expression for each item.
steps.whatToRemember: Whether one statement counts as one vow or two depends on whether the vow words were repeated for each item.

steps.title: He didn't know vows could be cancelled, so he may still cancel
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: someone who knew about vows but not that they can be cancelled may cancel once he finds out.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If he says 'I know there are vows, but I didn't know there are people who can cancel them,' he may cancel.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. A husband or father let the day pass without cancelling, and now explains that he didn't know he could cancel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally cancelling must happen on the day he hears the vow. Here his silence was not a real choice, because he didn't know he had the power to cancel. So his day starts when he learns of it.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מתניתין, marking the start of a משנה
Those who can cancel vows (husband or father)

phrases.english: MISHNA:
"I know that there are vows,
but I don't know that there are those who nullify",
he may nullify.
phrases.notes: He may cancel on the day he finds out, even though the day he heard the vow has already passed.

steps.triggerLanguage: יוֹדֵעַ אֲנִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ נְדָרִים אֲבָל אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁיֵּשׁ מְפִירִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Not knowing about the power to cancel allows a later הפרה.

steps.title: He didn't know it counted as a vow: רבי מאיר and חכמים argue
steps.stepSummary: If he knew about cancelling but didn't realize this was a vow, רבי מאיר says he can't cancel and חכמים say he can.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he says 'I know there are people who can cancel, but I didn't know this was a vow,' רבי מאיר says he may not cancel, and חכמים say he may cancel.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second case where the mistake is about the vow itself, and brings a disagreement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here he knew he had the power to cancel. He just didn't realize these words made a vow. רבי מאיר holds him to his silence. חכמים treat this mistake like the first case and let him cancel when he finds out.

phrases.english: "I know that there are those who nullify,
but I don't know that this is a vow",
Rabbi Meir says: he may not nullify,
and the Sages say: he may nullify.

steps.triggerLanguage: יוֹדֵעַ אֲנִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ מְפִירִין אֲבָל אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁזֶּה נֶדֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second kind of mistake that is debated, unlike the first case, which everyone agrees on.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Not knowing that something is a vow: רבי מאיר says no later הפרה, and חכמים say he may cancel.
steps.whatToRemember: Not knowing about the power to cancel lets him cancel later, and no one disagrees. Not knowing that it was a vow is debated: רבי מאיר says no, and חכמים say yes.

steps.title: A contradiction from the blind person who kills by accident
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a contradiction from a ברייתא. On the פסוק 'without seeing,' רבי יהודה says a blind person is left out, while רבי מאיר says a blind person is included.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: They raised a contradiction. The פסוק says 'without seeing' to leave out a blind person. These are the words of רבי יהודה. רבי מאיר says it comes to include the blind person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about an accidental killer who goes to an עיר מקלט to challenge the views in our משנה. It is only asking the question here. The answer will come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In our משנה, רבי מאיר does not let someone cancel when he was missing only part of the knowledge. He treats that person as if he knew. In the ברייתא, though, רבי מאיר treats a blind person, who never sees at all, the same as a seeing person who just didn't see this time, so both count as 'without seeing.' רבי יהודה, who is usually understood to be the חכמים who argue with רבי מאיר, seems to flip sides too.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה. It starts here.
'And they raised a contradiction.' The גמרא sets two sources against each other.
'Without seeing.' These are words from the פסוק about someone who kills by accident.
'To leave out a blind person.' The blind person is not included in the law.
'To include.' The פסוק is read as adding a case.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two topics. The blind killer has nothing to do with vows. The גמרא is only comparing how each תנא treats someone who was missing seeing or knowing.

phrases.english: GEMARA: And they raised a contradiction:
"Without seeing" — to exclude a blind person.
phrases.notes: במדבר 35:23. This is about someone who killed by accident and must run to an עיר מקלט.

phrases.english: These are the words of Rabbi Yehuda.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: לְרַבּוֹת אֶת הַסּוֹמֵא.
phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says: to include the blind person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It challenges the dispute between רבי מאיר and חכמים in step 8 by pointing to a ברייתא where they seem to hold the reverse.
steps.kashyaTarget: The positions of רבי מאיר and חכמים (רבי יהודה) in the משנה about someone who didn't realize this was a vow.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the משנה, רבי מאיר treats partial lack of knowledge as real knowledge, so he does tell different kinds of not-knowing apart. In the ברייתא, he lumps a fully blind person together with a momentary 'not seeing,' so he doesn't tell them apart. רבי יהודה seems reversed as well.
